subject: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set

messages.author: b063227c9709ab9e
messages.subject: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set
parts:
Hi there,


I conducted a yearlong (367 days) camera trap survey, with 11 camera trap sites which were in a fixed position throughout the survey. In order to allow for the data to be tested for demographic closure, and to run statistical analysis for a closed population, my project supervisor suggested that I split my data into four sessions of about 90 days/occassions each (session1 = occasions 1 -90; session2 = occasions 91 – 180; session3 = occasions 181 – 271; session4 = 272-367). 


How do I go about testing each session separately for closure (I have tried running multiple closure tests using different setups of the captfile and trapfile.


When I separate my captfile into the four different sessions and bring in my full trapfile (so not separated into the four sessions) I am able to run it for SB=FALSE and not SB=TRUE but I get the warning message saying:  In closure.test(BH_leftsecond, SB = FALSE, min.expected = 1) :  sum(fik) < 10

 

When I try run the closure test with the session specific captfile and session specific trapfile I get the error message Error in make.capthist(capt, trps, fmt = fmt, noccasions = noccasions,  :  fewer usage fields than max(occasion)

 

Once I have tested for closure and the four sessions are each closed, I want to join them and test them as one data file for population density and home range estimates.

 

Any help or guidance will be greatly appreciated.

 

Kind regards,

Jess

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set
parts:
Hi Jess,
A few comments:

I think the easiest way to test for closure violation within 90-day subsets of the total study duration would be to build the capthist object for the complete data set, then use subset.capthist() to divide the data into 4 separate data sets (not necessarily "sessions"), and then perform the test on each data set.

One of your error messages indicates that the number of usage fields doesn't match the number of occasions. As you split up your capture data, the associated trap file should have only the appropriate usage columns (e.g. for session 2 you would only include usage columns 91-180).  I think subset.capthist() would do this for you.

Note that if you test for closure within 90-day sessions and find no violation, then you can assume populations were closed within those 90-day sessions, but not that they were closed for the whole study period. If you plan to pool the data across all 367 days to estimate density, then you should test for closure across this whole time period.  Perhaps your supervisor was suggesting you divide the data into 4 sessions and estimate density separately for each (closed) session (perhaps using a robust design framework)?

I'm not sure if this is causing errors, but if you want to stick with "session", I think it would make sense to code your occasions as starting at occasion 1 within each session.

Good luck!
Eric

messages.subject: Re: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set
parts:
Hi Jessica,
These results seem indicate that the demographic closure assumption was not violated, but you should look into what that warning message means.  The tests may lack power to detect violations, and with an occasion for each day of sampling, capture probabilities will be very low, which might affect how the test performs.  Sorry I can't be more help. Reading relevant portions of the articles cited in the documentation for closure.test (particularly Stanley and Burnham 1999) is recommended.

Also, see http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.1676/full for left- and right- sided CR data!

Good luck,

Eric

parts:
That warning comes from my implementation of Otis et al. 1978 p 120, where they say
"If fk is large, the test statistic, can be assumed to be approximately distributed as a standard normal. (We have required that fk >= 10.)"
i.e. don't trust results with fk < 10. Reading their treatment of closure tests is still instructive.
Murray

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set
parts:
Hi Jess,
Switching to multimark might be useful to you in this case because of the left- and right-handed data, but won't solve the closure problem - all "closed-population" estimators, including those implemented in multimark, rely on the same assumption.  The tests for closure aren't perfect, and researchers often have to make the argument, based on the biology of the species or knowledge of the population sampled, that few additions or losses of individuals were likely to have occurred during sampling (e.g. because birth and death rates are low and dispersal is rare).  If that's not reasonable, you could use an open-population SECR model (Gardner et al. 2010 in Ecology), or estimate density from different temporal subsets of the data (seasons?) separately (possibly using the robust design framework), as discussed earlier.  These approaches would likely yield less precise estimates of density than a closed-population model, which is why people often use models that assume demographic closure even when they know the assumption was violated to some extent. 

I'll mention again that collapsing your data into longer occasions might help, and not just for the closure test, as very low occasion-specific capture probabilities might cause various methods to perform poorly.

Eric

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set
parts:
Jessica

It seems to me that the closure.test() warning message is a poor reason to abandon 'secr' (of course there may be other good reasons to do so!) (i) the message you are bothered by is only a warning not to take the p value at face value, (ii) any such test probably has low power, and is subject to many qualifications (I included closure.test() in 'secr' as a curiosity, not because I thought anyone should use it), and (iii) population turnover (non-closure) will bias SECR estimates, but intuitively the bias is proportional to the magnitude of the turnover, and will often be swamped by sampling error. A test for closure cannot really resolve the question of whether non-closure is a problem - that requires biological judgement, and possibly simulation of scenarios involving turnover. If there is enough turnover to distort the estimates then there are strategies you can use in 'secr' to correct this, such as subdividing the analysis into 'sessions' while constraining density to be constant across sessions.

I make these general points to set the record straight on SECR and 'secr'; I'm not trying to persuade you to stick with them if other methods better fit your problem.

Murray

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: closure test for multiple sessions made from one data set
parts:
Eric - I saw your good advice after I had hit 'send'. Your suggestion for temporal subsets corresponds to mine on subdividing into sessions. One catch there is that I think you can end up with spuriously narrower (not wider) confidence intervals because sessions are analysed as if they were each sampled from independent populations, rather than one 'realisation' with substantially the same individuals. Getting accurate CI without an open population SECR model probably requires parametric bootstrapping. Also, your point about lumping occasions to increase robustness has the ring of plausibility, but I wonder if there is any evidence for this? The model remains the same. I tackled Evan Cooch on this on phidot months ago and didn't get very far...
Murray

On Thu, Oct 22, 2015 at 3:48 AM, Eric H <ej...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
Hi Jess,
Switching to multimark might be useful to you in this case because of the left- and right-handed data, but won't solve the closure problem - all "closed-population" estimators, including those implemented in multimark, rely on the same assumption.  The tests for closure aren't perfect, and researchers often have to make the argument, based on the biology of the species or knowledge of the population sampled, that few additions or losses of individuals were likely to have occurred during sampling (e.g. because birth and death rates are low and dispersal is rare).  If that's not reasonable, you could use an open-population SECR model (Gardner et al. 2010 in Ecology), or estimate density from different temporal subsets of the data (seasons?) separately (possibly using the robust design framework), as discussed earlier.  These approaches would likely yield less precise estimates of density than a closed-population model, which is why people often use models that assume demographic closure even when they know the assumption was violated to some extent. 

I'll mention again that collapsing your data into longer occasions might help, and not just for the closure test, as very low occasion-specific capture probabilities might cause various methods to perform poorly.

Eric
